Title: On‐Orbit Fast Small Target Detection Method Based on the Improved YOLOv5 Model

Small target detection in remote sensing images is a challenging research ﬁeld. Real-time on-orbit small target detection is of great
signiﬁcance for rapid discovery and tracking of remote sensing targets. In this paper, the feasibility of automotive-grade system on
chips (SoC) to achieve on-orbit high-performance computing is analyzed, and a high-performance computing solution that meets
the complex space application environment is proposed. At the same time, based on the improved YOLOv5s (You Only Look
Once) model and the block parallel processing framework, a real-time on-orbit small target detection method for remote
sensing images is proposed. Under the conditions of limited computing resources on orbit, this method ensures the
eﬀectiveness of target detection while improving the speed of target detection. Experimental results show that the small target
detection time of this method is about 100 ms for a 5 × 3 k resolution image; meanwhile, the actual results for small object
detection with the improved model are also better than the original YOLOv5 model.
Keywords: on-orbit computing; remote sensing; target detection; YOLOv5
1. Introduction
Target detection technology is an important research ﬁeld in
satellite remote sensing applications and has been widely
used in environmental monitoring, precision agriculture,
geological disaster detection, and other ﬁelds. There have
been many research results on target detection methods for
diﬀerent application scenarios. Cheng and Han divided tar-
get detection methods into four categories: template match-
ing based, knowledge based, object-oriented image analysis
based, and machine learning based; they also analyzed and
compared the advantages and disadvantages of these
methods [1]. Among them, beneﬁting from powerful feature
extraction and classiﬁcation capabilities, deep learning
methods have achieved signiﬁcant improvements in object
detection and received more attention. Gui et al. analyzed
the application of deep learning methods on diﬀerent sensor
data such as optical images and synthetic aperture radar
(SAR); for example, both Mask R-CNN [2] and self-
attention methods have been successfully applied in object
detection research for optical and SAR data. This reﬂects
the wide adaptability of deep learning methods in the ﬁeld
of satellite remote sensing target detection [3]. For applica-
tions in the ﬁeld of earth observation, Hoeser et al. counted
the application examples of deep learning methods in the
ﬁelds of vehicle, ship, airport, and multicategory target
detection. Deep learning models based on convolutional
neural networks (CNNs) have been investigated across all
nine application categories. Diﬀerent applications corre-
spond to targets at varying scales, which reﬂect the eﬀective-
ness
of
deep
learning
methods
in
multiscale
target
detection [4].
Optical imaging sensors are the most widely used sen-
sors in the ﬁeld of satellite remote sensing. In the application
of satellite optical image target detection based on deep
learning methods, there are challenges such as multiscale
targets and small targets, which require a diﬀerent imple-
mentation method from conventional target detection [5].
To ensure the clarity of earth observation, satellite remote
sensing optical images are generally characterized by large

size and high resolution. Due to the long imaging distance,
targets such as aircraft and ships often have only dozens of
pixels in such images. The color, shape, and texture informa-
tion of these targets are not obvious, and their features are
easily obscured by complex background information. There-
fore, small target detection of large size images requires
more attention in the ﬁeld of satellite remote sensing [6,
7]. At present, the main solution is to adapt the general deep
learning model for small target detection. Li et al. improved
the Faster R-CNN [8] model based on the cross-layer atten-
tion mechanism and achieved a mAP of 74.3% on the public
DIOR dataset [9]. Qu et al. improved the SSD (single shot
multibox detector) [10] model based on dilated convolution
and feature fusion. The mAP on the remote sensing dataset
they designed was 76.51%, exceeding the 69.81% of the tradi-
tional SSD model [11]. The YOLO models [12] were designed
for both target detection accuracy and detection eﬃciency.
These models can be deployed on edge computing devices
with limited computing and storage resources, which are cur-
rently the dominant deep learning models in the ﬁeld of target
detection. Through appropriate improvements and enhance-
ments, the YOLO models have been widely used in the ﬁeld
of small target detection in remote sensing images. Xu and
Wu used DenseNet (densely connected network) to enhance
the feature extraction capability of YOLOv3 and improved
its mAP by 12.12% for small target detection such as airplanes
[13]. Yang et al. modiﬁed the YOLOv4 network structure and
loss function and added a coordinate attention mechanism.
The mAP on the RSOD dataset was 95.03%, exceeding the
original YOLOv4’s 92.08% and the Faster R-CNN network
model [14]. Other versions of the YOLO models have also
been improved for small target detection, for such methods
based on YOLOv5 [15], YOLOv7 [16], and YOLOv8 [17].
These works reﬂect the application potential of the YOLO
models in the ﬁeld of small target detection.
Real-time performance serves as a critical metric for target
detection in remote sensing images. The conventional ground
station–based processing approach of remote sensing images
suﬀers from transmission latency, while the downlink of large
size image data also faces challenges in link availability. Real-
time object detection in remote sensing images based on deep
learning relies on on-orbit intelligent computing. However,
due to constraints in weight, size, power consumption, and
radiation environment, mature deep learning methods and
high-performance computing platforms cannot be directly
deployed in space systems [18]. Bing analyzed the current
statuses of intelligent remote sensing satellite platforms, pay-
loads, computing resources, and communications and pro-
posed the timeliness of remote sensing data, imbalanced data
distribution, and large-capacity storage issues that need to be
solved [19]. Yin et al. comprehensively analyzed the advan-
tages of on-orbit intelligent computing. In the example of
disaster detection, the transmission of useless data by 50%
was reduced by on-orbit intelligent computing [20]. Diana
and Dini comprehensively discussed the hardware devices
and software technologies for onboard computing that sup-
port neural network applications. Various types of devices
are being explored in the ﬁeld of onboard computing, includ-
ing systems using ASIC (application-speciﬁc integrated cir-
cuit) devices (such as Intel Movidius Myriad and NVIDIA
Jetson boards), FPGA (ﬁeld programmable gate array) based,
and using neuromorphic hardware and memristors. In addi-
tion, commercial solutions that meet radiation resistance have
also made great progress [21]. These devices vary in comput-
ing eﬃciency, power consumption, radiation resistance, and
software ecosystem, which should be selected based on diﬀer-
ent satellite missions.
Due to their cost and well-established ecosystem, ASICs,
generally as commercial oﬀ-the-shelf (COTS) devices, have
emerged as a research focus for on-orbit intelligent comput-
ing through radiation hardening. Murphy et al. conducted a
comparative analysis of three embedded computing modu-
les—NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX (graphics processing unit,
GPU), Huawei Atlas 200 (neural network processing unit,
NPU), and Intel Movidius Myriad X (video processing unit,
VPU)—demonstrating signiﬁcant variations in computa-
tional capability and power consumption that necessitate
careful selection based on speciﬁc mission requirements
[22]. Φ-Sat-1 is the ﬁrst satellite to use an on-orbit deep neu-
ral network for earth observation. The satellite uses the Intel
Movidius Myriad 2 VPU (1 TOPS, 1 W) as a network accel-
erator and uses the U-Net [23] model to achieve cloud seg-
mentation based on multispectral images [24]. Through
on-orbit processing, Φ-Sat-1 avoids 30% of useless data from
being transmitted to the ground [25]. Φ-Sat-2 also uses
Movidius Myriad 2 VPU as the onboard computing plat-
form. Guerrisi et al. designed an AI-based image compression
model which is called the CAE (convolutional autoencoder)
model. They compared the performance of the model on
VPU (Intel Movidius Myriad 2), GPU (NVIDIA GeForce
GTX 1650), and central processing unit (CPU) (Intel Core
i7-6700), where VPU had the lowest power consumption
(1.4 vs. 83 vs. 45.5W), but the longest running time (10.92
vs. 0.95 vs. 1.9s) [26]. FPGAs have also been investigated for
space applications, demonstrating promising potential in
onboard data processing [27]. Rapuano et al. compared the
performance of Xilinx Kintex Ultrascale XQRKU060 FPGA
and Intel Myriad 2 VPU by accelerating the CloudScout
CNN model. In terms of inference time, FPGA is stronger
than VPU (264.7 vs. 346ms), but the power estimation value
of FPGA exceeds that of VPU [28]. Cratere et al. used Xilinx
Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC FPGA to run four diﬀerent CNN
models to verify the feasibility of FPGA for on-orbit cloud
detection. The FPGA-accelerated pruned SceneNet model
and the VPU-accelerated CloudScout CNN model showed a
slight improvement in detection accuracy and power con-
sumption (98.4% vs. 92.0%, 2.8 vs. 1.8W), but a signiﬁcant
reduction in inference time (17.5 vs. 81.3ms), demonstrating
the advantages of FPGA for onboard computing [29]. Fang
et al. used the improved YOLOv5s model for on-orbit small
target detection in infrared thermal imaging. They used Xilinx
Zynq 7020 as the experimental platform and compared the
performance of GPU (NVIDIA RTX 4060) and CPU (Intel
i9-13900) acceleration. FPGA achieved the best energy eﬃ-
ciency ratio (3.64 vs. 1.15 vs. 0.85) [30]. Compared with COTS
ASICs, FPGAs have stronger radiation resistance and better
computing eﬃciency, but they are inferior in software ecosys-
tem and take a longer time to deploy applications.

Many remote sensing applications need to solve prob-
lems such as rapid target discovery and tracking. Related
methods need to consider both the accuracy and real-time
performance of small target detection. At present, research
work in this area mainly focuses on the accuracy of small
target detection, which often increases computational com-
plexity, and few studies discuss the problem of on-orbit
real-time target detection in remote sensing images. How-
ever, due to the limitation of on-orbit computing resources,
real-time target detection in remote sensing images requires
the optimization of algorithms. This paper ﬁrst analyzes the
application of automotive-grade COTS SoCs in real-time
detection of remote sensing targets and proposes an on-
orbit high-performance parallel processing framework. Sec-
ondly, by lightweighting the YOLOv5s model and avoiding
large size image scaling, an on-orbit detection method for
satellite remote sensing that takes into account both perfor-
mance and eﬃciency is implemented. The paper is orga-
nized as follows: The second section is the selection of the
onboard computing platform; the third section is the design
of the parallel processing method; the fourth section is the
improvement of the YOLOv5s model; the ﬁfth section is
the experimental results and analysis; the ﬁnal section con-
cludes the work of the paper.
2. On-Orbit Computing Based on Automotive-
Grade SoCs
Radiation-resistant SoCs generally have limited computing
resources.
The
DMIPS
number
of
the
widely
used
radiation-resistant SoC GR740 is 1836 [31]. The RAD5545,
the highest performance CPU in the PowerPC architecture,
only has 5600 DMIPS [32]. COTS SoCs are better solutions
for on-orbit high-performance computing. The researchers
of Jet Propulsion Laboratory analyze the Snapdragon 855
SoC that has been used on the International Space Station.
The DMIPS number of its CPU subsystem is 138,255, far
exceeding the 1836 of the radiation-resistant GR740. In
addition, its GPU and NPU subsystems provide 950
GFLOPS/FP32 and 7 TOPS/INT8 computing performance,
respectively [33]. Snapdragon 855 can adapt to most image
classiﬁcation models such as MSL1 and ResNet50, and its
reasoning performance is better than Myriad 2 [33]. Tsin-
ghua University’s Q-SAT satellite uses an embedded GPU
with a computing performance of 1.33 TFLOPS. It veriﬁes
the feasibility of on-orbit detection of remote sensing targets
through the YOLOv3-tiny model [34]. However, the high-
resolution characteristics of the images are not taken into
account. Among the many COTS devices, the automotive-
grade SoCs are a highly prioritized category which comply
with the AEC-Q100 automotive reliability speciﬁcation and
ISO 26262 automotive functional safety speciﬁcation. The
AEC-Q100 speciﬁcation ensures that electronic components
can operate reliably over the long term in harsh working
environments, which is like the requirements of aerospace
applications. For example, the operating temperature range
speciﬁed in AEC-Q100 meets the environmental tempera-
ture requirements for low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites. Addi-
tionally, its self-recovery requirements for latch-up eﬀects
are also of signiﬁcant value in protecting against single-
event eﬀects (SEEs) in space environments. The ISO 26262
speciﬁcation imposes requirements on hazard analysis and
risk management for the entire electronic system, while also
governing design methods and processes. The automotive-
grade SoCs are the preferred device for the European Space
Agency’s onboard Q1 device category [35].
Automotive-grade SoCs need to enhance their ability to
radiation resistance in aerospace applications. Radiation
experiments show that although the built-in GPU, NPU,
and CPU of the automotive-grade SA8155P are aﬀected by
SEE, the probability of SEE is small [36]. In terms of total
ionizing dose (TID) eﬀect, the SA8155P has a certain ability
to radiation resistance; a 1 mm thick aluminum shell shield-
ing protection can ensure the 5-year life cycle of the
SA8155P in LEO [37]. The daily occurrence rate of SEE of
NVIDIA Xavier NX in LEO and geostationary orbit is also
at a low level of 10−2 [38]. Through radiation-resistant tech-
nologies such as hardware redundancy, memory protection,
software protection [39], and shell shielding methods,
automotive-grade SoCs can eﬀectively avoid the impact of
SEE and TID. Real-time monitoring of the operating status
of COTS devices through radiation-resistant devices can fur-
ther improve the reliable working ability of automotive-
grade devices under the inﬂuence of SEE and TID [40].
Automotive-grade component vendors typically exclu-
sively serve automotive manufacturers and are not available
to general consumers. The BST A1000, a high-performance
automotive SoC developed by Black Sesame Technologies
(BST) for autonomous driving applications, breaks this con-
vention by oﬀering accessibility to general-purpose AI com-
puting users. We therefore employ the BST A1000 as our
hardware evaluation platform in this research. The A1000
complies with AEC-Q100 Grade 2 and ISO26262 ASIL-B
speciﬁcations; it adopts a hybrid structure with CPU+NPU.
The CPU subsystem of the A1000 consists of 8 ARM Cortex
A55 processors. The NPU subsystem provides common oper-
ators for deep learning and achieves a computing performance
of 48 TOPS/1.2GHz. The A1000 supports INT8, INT16, and
FP16 quantization modes, enabling dynamic precision selec-
tion based on real-time performance and accuracy require-
ments. The quad-core NPU architecture of the A1000
enables parallel execution of multiple models, allowing simul-
taneous processing of multiple images during object detection
tasks. The power consumption of the A1000 is less than 8W
and has an energy eﬃciency ratio of more than 5TOPS/W.
Compared with the SA8155P that has been used in aerospace
applications, the A1000 provides nearly seven times perfor-
mance improvement at almost the same power consumption.
Therefore, it is more suitable for on-orbit intelligent comput-
ing. The comparison of the A1000, SA8155P, and Xavier NX
is shown in Table 1.
3. Block Parallel Processing of Large
Size Images
Due to resource constraints, deep learning models for object
detection inherently impose certain limitations on the input
image size during implementation. For larger images, the

model will downscale them at the input stage. However,
image scaling will lead to the loss of pixel information, and
the image details of small targets will be blurred or even lost
after the scaling process. This pixel loss will directly aﬀect
the detection performance of the model, making it diﬃcult
to accurately detect and locate small targets. This paper
adopts an image tiling strategy to reduce the pixel loss
caused by image scaling. By dividing the large size image
into smaller subimages to avoid image scaling by the model,
the pixel information of small targets can be retained to the
maximum extent. The NPU of A1000 supports parallel pro-
cessing of multiple models with multiple cores, by which
multiple subimages can ensure the synchronization of the
same image processing and improve computational eﬃ-
ciency. In the experiments of this paper, the height and
width of a large size image are divided equally, and four sub-
images of equal size are used for parallel detection of small
targets.
Two special cases of tiling a large size image need to be
handled. The ﬁrst is that the target is exactly on the sub-
image boundary. When this occurs, the target will appear
in two subimages, which will lead to missed detection of
the target. To address this issue, subimages cannot be simply
partitioned at the boundary positions but instead require a
certain overlapping region between adjacent subimages.
Assume the original image has a width of W pixels and
height of H pixels, with an overlap stride of O (O > 0) pixels
between subimages. The pixel coordinates of the top-left
corners of the four subimages (top left, bottom left, top right,
and bottom right) in the original image, along with their
width and height, are as follows: (0,0,W/2+O,H/2+O),
(0,H/2-O,W/2+O,H),
(W/2-O,0,W,H/2+O),
and
(W/2-
O,H/2-O,W,H).
The presence of parameter O creates overlapping
regions between subimages. While a larger O value can pre-
vent target loss caused by image tiling, it simultaneously
increases inference time and is detrimental to real-time
detection performance. In small target detection applica-
tions, the overlapping area does not need to be set too large.
By the overlapping area, targets across subimages will not be
missed, which ensures the integrity and accuracy of the
detection.
After completing the small target detection in each sub-
image, the detection results of diﬀerent subimages are seam-
lessly aligned on the original image by adjusting the
coordinates, thereby restoring the complete detection results.
However, due to the existence of overlapping areas, the same
target may be detected simultaneously on subimages. The
nonmaximum suppression (NMS) [41] algorithm is used to
ﬁlter the prediction boxes in the overlapping areas. The
NMS algorithm sorts the conﬁdence value of each prediction
box and calculates the intersection over union (IoU) between
overlapping prediction boxes. When the IoU values of pre-
diction boxes exceed the preset threshold, only the prediction
box with higher conﬁdence is retained, and the prediction
boxes with lower conﬁdence are suppressed. By NMS, the
detection results in the overlapping area are accurate and
nonredundant.
Since there are overlapping areas in the subimage, the
second special case is that the target is partially predicted
in one subimage and fully predicted in another subimage.
A boundary ﬁltering mechanism by which these incomplete
prediction boxes are ﬁltered is designed by setting a certain
threshold. Given a subimage where the top-left coordinates
of a predicted bounding box are Bx and Bγ, the bottom-
right pixel coordinates of the subimage are Ex and Eγ. The
ﬁltering mechanism is as follows:
if Ex −Bx ≤T,
drop
if Ey −By ≤T,
drop
Else,
keep

Here, parameter T denotes the distance threshold
between the edge of a predicted bounding box and the sub-
image boundary. A smaller value of T yields more precise
ﬁltering of part detections, while a larger T may eliminate
valid detections. However, due to overlapping regions
between subimages, no ultimate detection loss occurs. For
small object detection, T should be relatively small and must
satisfy T < O. In this paper, O = 80; T = 10. If there is a
prediction box with a distance of less than 10 pixels from
the boundary, the current prediction box is incomplete and
will be ﬁltered out. The complete block parallel processing
is presented in Figure 1.
Figure 1 demonstrates that through the processing of
two special cases in parallel tiled detection and subsequent
NMS reﬁnement, we obtain unambiguous and nonredun-
dant detection results for small targets.
4. Improving YOLOv5s Model
GPU-based computing platforms can rapidly adapt to vari-
ous new algorithm versions due to CUDA’s robust software
ecosystem and strong versatility. In contrast, FPGA- and
NPU-based platforms exhibit superior energy eﬃciency
ratios, but their relatively closed software ecosystems restrict
compatibility to speciﬁc model versions. The YOLOv5 [42]
is a deep learning model that is designed for target detection
by giving consideration to both accuracy and speed and is
suitable
for
deployment
on
low-power
edge
devices.
Recently, diﬀerent improved versions of the YOLOv5 model
have been used in the ﬁeld of small target detection in
remote sensing images [43, 44]. YOLOv5 has demonstrated
excellent compatibility across multiple hardware platforms
with the ability to export to multiple formats. BST A1000
has achieved optimized performance through platform-

speciﬁc adaptations with the YOLOv5 model. YOLOv5 con-
sists of multiple models with diﬀerent parameter values that
range from 1.9 to 86.7 million. On the COCO dataset, the
corresponding mAP0.5 values are 45.7–68.9. Considering
the computing performance of A1000, the YOLOv5s model
is chosen to be deployed. The YOLOv5s model has 7.3 mil-
lion parameters, and the mAP0.5 value is 56.8 on the COCO
dataset.
The YOLOv5s model consists of three parts: the back-
bone, neck, and head. The backbone network extracts fea-
tures of images with diﬀerent scales through the down-
sampling process, and the neck part obtains feature maps
with equal resolution through the up-sampling process and
sends them to the head part, which obtains the results
through convolution operation. In the YOLOv5s model, in
order to ensure the accuracy of multiscale object detection,
a ﬁve-level down-sampling process from 2× to 32× is
adopted in the down-sampling stage of the backbone net-
work. In the up-sampling stage of the neck part of YOLOv5s,
reverse processing is performed to output the results after
8×, 16×, and 32× down-sampling. However, in the case of
small target detection in large size images, the small target
features will disappear after 16× and 32× down-sampling.
Therefore, it does not make sense to further process the
feature results after 16× and 32× down-sampling in the neck
part and output the results of the corresponding resolution
in the head part. However, the number of feature maps in
this part is large, and the corresponding processing will have
a signiﬁcant impact on the inference time. Therefore, in
order to lighten the model, the 16× and 32× down-
sampling processes are pruned in the neck part. Corre-
spondingly, the head part of the YOLOv5 model needs to
be adjusted accordingly. The YOLOv5s model and its light-
weight improvement are shown in Figure 2.
In Figure 2, C3 and SPPF are network modules deﬁned
by the YOLOv5 model. The gray part of Figure 2 is mainly
used for the detection of medium and large objects. This part
is pruned to meet the lightweight requirements of small tar-
get detection. Comparison with the original model, the back-
bone network of improved YOLOv5s remains as it is, and its
multiscale feature extraction capability is retained. The up-
sampling process of the neck part has not changed, and only
the output processing part of the 16× and 32× down-
sampling results has been pruned, so the output of the 8×
down-sampling result is not aﬀected. Based on this pruning
process, the head part also only retains the convolution cal-
culation of the 8× down-sampling result. After model prun-
ing, the model parameters are reduced to 4.8 million, which
is 34.2% lower than the original model. This lightweight
improvement of the model speeds up the model’s reasoning
while ensuring target detection performance. By reducing
the amount of calculation and the complexity of the feature
maps, the model is more eﬃcient during reasoning, thereby
improving overall operating eﬃciency.
To further improve the computational eﬃciency of the
YOLOv5s model, we preset six anchor boxes for the model
on the 8× down-sample feature maps. These anchor boxes
are obtained by clustering the marker boxes in the dataset
with the k-means clustering algorithm [45]. The k-means
algorithm optimizes the size and shape of each anchor by
minimizing the matching error between the anchor box
and the target marker box, so that these anchor boxes can
more eﬀectively cover the range of changes in the target
object. In this paper, the distance metric of the k-means
algorithm is deﬁned as follows:

5. Experiments
5.1. Dataset Construction. The improved DOTA-v2.0 dataset
[46] is used to verify the small target detection method in
this paper. First, ﬁve speciﬁc small target categories in
the dataset are screened and retained, namely, “small vehi-
cle, large vehicle, ship, plane, and helicopter.” These cate-
gories are selected mainly based on their commonness in
remote sensing images and their importance in practical
applications.
Second, for further improving the diversity of the dataset
and enhancing the robustness of the model, and to avoid
image scaling, the original images in the training set are
processed in blocks. The selection of subimage size needs
to be carefully considered. On the one hand, smaller subi-
mages increase the number of sample images; each subimage
is
enhanced
through

matched. This method not only eﬀectively increases the size
of the dataset but also helps to improve the model’s percep-

task.
After the above processing, the size of the dataset has
been signiﬁcantly expanded. The number of samples in the
training set increases from the original 1.8 K images to
25 K images, while the number of samples in the validation
set increases from 0.5 to 7 K. This expansion eﬀectively
increases the diversity of training data, which in turn facili-
tates model training, reduces the risk of overﬁtting, and
enhances the generalization ability of the model.
5.2. Model Training. The model is implemented in PyTorch
and trained using an NVIDIA 3080 Ti GPU. The image
input size of the model is set to 1024 × 1024. To improve
the robustness and generalization ability of the model, the
training images are enhanced in various ways, such as trans-
lation, left-right ﬂipping, and mosaic. In addition, multiscale
training is enabled during training, which allows adjust-
ments of plus or minus 50% based on the original input size.
The batch size of the training process is set to 8, the opti-
mizer is the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm,
and the initial learning rate is set to 0.01. The learning rate
decay strategy is adopted in model training, in which the
learning rate is reduced every 50 epochs to ensure that the
model converges more stably in the later stages of training.
At the same time, the momentum term is set to 0.9 to accel-
erate convergence and reduce oscillation. To prevent overﬁt-
ting, the training process adopts an early stopping strategy;
that is, the training is stopped when the accuracy does not
improve within a few epochs. The cross-validation is used
in the training process to ensure that the model performs

impact of removing 16× and 32× down-sample feature maps
on the detection performance of small target objects, we

5.5. Experimental Results of A1000 Platform. Model deploy-
ment on the A1000 platform requires the shanhai deploy-
ment toolchain. The shanhai deployment toolchain is a set
of easy-to-use software development tools developed by
BST for their AI chips. The toolchain can recompile the
model implemented in PyTorch into a model that can adapt
to the A1000 platform. During the model training process,
the toolchain also provides quantization level, model prun-
ing, operator fusion, and other performance optimization
tools, which can obtain the desired model parameters
through multiple iterative training. Considering the compu-
tational eﬃciency, the 8-bit integer quantization mode was
adopted. In the experiment, the actual image size used for
target detection is 4960 × 2912; the images of this size cannot
be directly input into the model for inference on the A1000
platform, whose maximum image size that can be directly
processed is 4096 × 2400. To reduce the computational load
caused by too many overlapping areas, the original image is
evenly divided in height and width, and each original image
is divided into four subimages of equal size. The actual sub-
image size is set to 2560 × 1536, by which the overlapping
area of the subimages is 80 pixels in both height and width.
The model input resolution is also set to 2560 × 1536 to pre-
serve image details as much as possible; that is, no scaling is
performed for subimages. The subimages are directly input
into the model to achieve small target detection. On the
A1000 platform, two improved YOLOv5s models run in
parallel, and the batch size of each model is set to 2; that
is, every two subimages are processed sequentially by one
model to ensure the synchronization of the entire high-
resolution image processing. The block preprocessing of
high-resolution images and the postprocessing of inference
results are completed by the A1000 CPU. Table 4 shows
the inference speed of processing.
From the data in Table 4, we can see that the improved
model reduces the inference time by about 30 ms. That is,
the inference time is improved by 22.7%.

6. Conclusions
Although the automotive-grade SoC based on the NPU
architecture has the disadvantage of limited model adapta-
tion compared with the GPU hardware platform, it is still
the preferred choice for on-orbit intelligent computing
platforms due to its excellent energy eﬃciency and long-
term reliability. The YOLO series models, including the
YOLOv5 model, have been extensively studied in the ﬁeld
of remote sensing target detection. Based on the character-
istics of the automotive-grade SoC BST A1000, this paper
provides an accurate remote sensing small target detection
method with an inference time of 100 ms through a light-
weight YOLOv5s model and a block parallel processing
mechanism. The experimental results verify the eﬀective-
ness of this method. The research of this paper compre-
hensively considers the diﬃculties of on-orbit computing
and rapid detection of remote sensing small targets, which
provide an engineering-implementable on-orbit remote
sensing small target detection solution that takes into
account both inference performance and speed.
The work of the paper is mainly to reduce the computa-
tional complexity as much as possible without aﬀecting the
performance of small target detection, thereby improving
the inference speed. However, since the intelligent comput-
ing platform based on the NPU architecture cannot provide
a general implementation framework for deep learning
models, it is very diﬃcult to compare the performance of
the improved model with other models, especially the latest
models, which often depend on the toolchain provided by
the manufacturer. Given that new models in the YOLO
series, such as YOLOv11 [47] which have improved perfor-
mance and eﬃciency, our next step is to study the adapta-
tion and optimization of the new models on the A1000
platform.
